**Verdict:** Paul Graham would almost certainly be against it. The product sells exactly the thing he thinks AI is wrecking, which is the pressure on people to learn to write and therefore to think. It only works if the essay deceives the college reading it, so it is not the empathy-driven kind of startup he says makes founders rich.

**Based on:** follows from what he said (confidence: medium). He never discusses admission essays in the vault, and the vault has no `thinking/pg` page, so this rests on two close essays.

**How we get there**
1. **The nearest case he addressed is AI writing for people.** In *Writes and Write-Nots* ([paulgraham.com/writes.html](https://paulgraham.com/writes.html)) he says the old pressure to write was what made people learn: "if you couldn't buy or steal words, you had to write them yourself. And as a result nearly everyone who was expected to write had to learn how." Then: "Not anymore. AI has blown this world open. Almost all pressure to write has dissipated." He calls the result bad, because "writing is thinking," and a world of writes and write-nots "will be a world of thinks and think-nots." ([[web-14f0078fb455]])
2. **He puts paying someone to write for you in the same group as plagiarism.** He mentions people who "pay someone to write for you, like JFK, or plagiarize, like MLK" as the old ways around writing yourself. A paid AI admission essay is the cheap, mass-market form of both.
3. **His rule for startups is that they win by making customers better off, not by exploiting anyone.** In *How to Earn a Billion Dollars* ([paulgraham.com/earn.html](https://paulgraham.com/earn.html)) he says "the key is not exploitation but empathy," and concedes that "There are other ways to get rich than by starting startups. Some of those do require you to exploit people." ([[web-278ac10fa14b]]) In *Making Startups Powerful* ([paulgraham.com/powerful.html](https://paulgraham.com/powerful.html)) he says every move "has to make things better for the customer." ([[web-19ac0b6d18d2]])
4. **Applied to this case:** the student gets an outcome but skips the one exercise in the application that makes them think about themselves. The college is deceived about who wrote it. That puts the business on the wrong side of both rules: it helps students give up writing, and it makes money by misleading a third party.

**Why he'd say it**
- "To write well you have to think clearly, and thinking clearly is hard." ([[web-14f0078fb455]]) A 17-year-old who outsources this essay misses one of the few times they're forced to do that.
- "There will still be smart people, but only those who choose to be." ([[web-14f0078fb455]]) This startup's business is helping people choose not to.
- "You can only do these things when the result is better for the customer." ([[web-19ac0b6d18d2]])

**What would change his answer:** a product that makes students write better themselves, such as an AI tutor that questions and critiques their draft but doesn't write it. That fits his view that you should still learn to write, so he'd likely judge it on ordinary startup grounds. The inference could also break on market size: if colleges start openly assuming AI help, the deception part goes away. The "writing is thinking" objection would still stand.

*Not in the vault:* elsewhere, PG has written that college admissions matter less than students think. That suggests a second objection: the product optimizes something that isn't worth optimizing.

**Verdict:** No, not on the strength of the plan. To Paul Graham, a year spent writing a business plan before building anything is a warning sign: the founder has been working on a story for investors when they should have been building a product for users. What could still get them funded is anything they've built, then or since.

**Based on:** follows from what he said (confidence: high). He has never talked about this exact founder, but his August 2026 essay addresses business plans directly.

**How we get there**
1. **Business plans.** He calls business plan competitions "not merely useless but positively misleading. It trains founders to think that fundraising is the essential step in starting a startup" ([[web-c75e015ff81a]], https://paulgraham.com/prepare.html).
2. **The rule behind it.** "The people you need to impress are users, not investors, and the way you impress them is with prototypes, not words." ([[web-c75e015ff81a]])
3. **Applied to this founder.** A year of planning with nothing built is the "words, not prototypes" mistake carried on for twelve months. It also fails the test YC actually uses (below).

**Why he'd say it**
- **The selection test is building.** "What do the YC partners look for? It's surprisingly simple. They want people who are good at building things and have a habit of doing it." ([[web-c75e015ff81a]]) A year with nothing built is evidence against that habit.
- **His fix is the reverse of a business plan.** "Instead of thinking about startups without building anything, they should be building things without thinking about whether they'll turn into startups." ([[web-c75e015ff81a]])
- **You learn this by doing it.** "The only way to learn how to start a startup is to do it." ([[web-c75e015ff81a]])
- **Speed still matters, even with AI.** "we have all these powerful AI tools and there's still a lot of startups in this batch that are not shipping fast enough." ([[yt-5bxp78i96S8]] @ 16:04, https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=5bxp78i96S8&t=964s)
- **YC was set up for founders without a plan.** Jessica Livingston says that in 2005, VCs wanted a business plan and a tested idea. YC was meant to write a small check "just so a Founder can sort of quit their job pay the rent and test out if their idea even works" ([[yt-6u4JVz7iQTY]] @ 2:50, https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=6u4JVz7iQTY&t=170s). This is Livingston speaking, not PG.
- **Other YC partners say the same.** Michael Seibel: "spending all that time on a pitch deck is not as valuable as spending your time building anything that you can give to a customer" ([[yt-1hHMwLxN6EM]] @ 11:11, https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1hHMwLxN6EM&t=671s).

**What would change his answer:** The founder ships something quickly and real users want it. At that point the year of planning is a sunk cost, and he'd judge them on building speed, empathy for users and formidability, like any other founder. The inference is weakest for regulated or hard-tech startups, where the vault notes you can't launch as fast and some planning before building is necessary.

**Verdict:** He'd tell them to stop being remote and get the founders into one place, ideally Silicon Valley, at least for a while. His case for startups rests on people being near each other, and co-founders in different time zones are about as far apart as founders can get.

**Based on:** follows from what he said (confidence: medium). The vault has nothing from him on remote work or time zones. I searched both the wiki and the raw transcripts for "remote", "time zone", "in person" and "office" and found nothing relevant. This answer applies his views on location and co-founders to your case.

**How we get there**
1. **The nearest case he addressed is where to locate a startup.** In Stockholm (April 2026) he said the answer to "Should I go there?" is "the same now as it always is. Yes, you should." ([yt-QHJkUw31YX8 @ 0:36](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=QHJkUw31YX8&t=36s)). He thinks the main payoff is unplanned contact: "if you're working on something ambitious, there's nothing in the world that's better than serendipitous meetings with people who are working on the same stuff" (@ [3:20](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=QHJkUw31YX8&t=200s)). He also says that "Maybe planned meetings lop off the outliers."
2. **The rule behind it:** good things happen when ambitious people are close together. In his words, people "egg one another on" and things "move faster" (@ [3:53](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=QHJkUw31YX8&t=233s)). Separately, he says the only way to know whether a co-founder works is to have actually worked with them: "the only way to tell for sure if someone will be good to work with is to work with them" ([prepare.html](https://paulgraham.com/prepare.html)).
3. **How this case fits the rule:** co-founders in different time zones get almost no unplanned contact, even with each other. Each conversation has to be scheduled, which is the planned-meeting mode he thinks "lops off the outliers." The time-zone gap also cuts the hours they can work side by side, which is how he thinks co-founders really get to know each other.

**Why he'd say it**
- Companies don't just need talent, they need people together in one place. Talking about cities, he says "All you need is a place founders want to live and a critical mass of them" ([yt-QHJkUw31YX8 @ 21:09](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=QHJkUw31YX8&t=1269s)).
- He cites YC's data that startups that go home after YC are "only about half as likely to become unicorns" (@ 18:57). He discounts that number for selection bias, but it still points the same way.
- He says that "starting a startup is normally a very lonely business," and his remedy is a batch that works like an office full of peers ([yt-5bxp78i96S8 @ 17:11](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=5bxp78i96S8&t=1031s)). Splitting the founders across time zones makes the loneliness worse.
- He tells founders to pick co-founders as they'd pick friends, people "you have known long enough to be sure" ([yt-ii1jcLg-eIQ @ 4:38](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ii1jcLg-eIQ&t=278s)). That's harder to judge when you rarely share a room.

**What he's done:** YC used to fly its Boston-batch startups out to Silicon Valley for a second demo day (@ 7:43). One of the English startups he invested in outside YC moved to the Valley (@ 12:47).

**What would change his answer:** The analogy breaks if the co-founders have a long history of building things together, since then the "know them well enough" test is already passed. It also breaks if their customers are spread around the world and there's no one city they'd gain from being in. Even then, from his reasoning I'd expect him to say "at least do YC together in person, then decide." That last line is my extrapolation, not something he said. Also, these talks come from YC's founder, who admits he is "talking my own book" when he recommends coming to the Valley.

Beyond the vault: his older essays on startup hubs make the same case for being in one place. The vault hasn't captured them yet, so I haven't quoted them.

**Verdict:** Probably not. He'd most likely tell you to raise a normal seed round, sized to reach your next milestone, from investors whose only interest is your equity. If Google matters to you, have them as a customer or a partner, not as a large shareholder. A big strategic check ties your company to another company's interests, and his 2026 advice is to look for ways *not* to be held back by other companies.

**Based on:** follows from what he said (confidence: medium). The vault has no PG statement about strategic or corporate investors, and searches of both the wiki and the raw sources for "strategic", "corporate" and "raise too much" found nothing. This answer applies his rules to a case he didn't address.

**How we get there**
1. **The nearest case he did address.** In office hours, he asks what would make a company *more powerful*, not how it could get more money: "Often what you're doing when you explore ways to make a company more powerful is finding ways not to be held back by other companies." ([[web-19ac0b6d18d2]], https://paulgraham.com/powerful.html). He even turns this into a test: "In what ways is the current idea being held back by other companies?"
2. **The rule behind it.** Taking money is the "incremental" kind of thinking. Becoming independent of other companies is the kind that changes how big the company can get. He says money-thinking "tends to yield incremental improvements" ([[web-19ac0b6d18d2]]).
3. **Why it applies here.** A large seed check from Google mainly gets you money. In return, a company whose interests differ from yours becomes a big holder in your startup at the earliest stage. By his own test, that is a way of being held back by another company, which is what he wants founders to get rid of.

**Why he'd say it**
- **The alignment between investor and founder breaks.** His reason that investors and founders want the same thing is that investors simply own a share: "If they get what they want, you get what you want, so that's why investors want people who are formidable." ([[yt-5bxp78i96S8]] @ 9:57, https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=5bxp78i96S8&t=597s). A financial investor fits that. A strategic investor also has its own goals, like product direction, a possible acquisition, or competitive information, so your wins aren't automatically its wins.
- **You don't need a big round at seed.** "you adjust for how much money you've got" and "As long as you can get to some kind of milestone, then you can convince investors to give you more." ([[yt-5bxp78i96S8]] @ 11:37 / 12:09, https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=5bxp78i96S8&t=697s). Raising only enough for the next milestone makes "big" unnecessary, even before you consider the "strategic" part.
- **Growth is what gets you good investors.** "the best way to convince investors, is to start a startup that's actually doing well … and then simply tell investors so." ([[yt-ii1jcLg-eIQ]] @ 9:51). If you're growing, you don't need a corporate investor to vouch for you.
- *Wider YC view (Caldwell and Seibel, not PG):* leverage means being able to walk away from a deal ([[yt-7TU636F_yVQ]] @ 13:23). Seibel's example of the naive founder is the one who thinks "someone from Google emailed me … We made it" and pins everything on that one deal (@ 11:09). A big Google stake at seed creates exactly that kind of dependence.

**What would change his answer**
- **Google's money comes with no special rights.** That means no right of first refusal on an acquisition, no exclusivity, and no board seat or special access to information. Google would then be an investor that just owns a share, which passes his alignment test. Even so, he'd probably still say to raise only what the next milestone needs.
- **Google's involvement makes the product much better for customers.** An example is distribution or infrastructure you couldn't get any other way. He puts one condition on every move that makes a company more powerful: "They all have to make things better for the customer." But this argues for a partnership, not necessarily a big equity stake.

Outside the vault, YC folk wisdom commonly warns about strategic investors at seed: they can scare off Google's competitors as buyers and partners, they send a signal to other VCs, and they can limit who can buy you later. I can't attribute that to PG from this vault, so treat it as general background, not as his words.

**Verdict:** Paul Graham would be skeptical. He'd say a patent isn't an advantage on its own. What counts is whether you've made something people want so much that it grows fast. A startup that leans on legal protection instead is playing the wrong game.

**Based on:** follows from what he said (confidence: medium). Nothing in the vault mentions patents as a startup strategy. The answer comes from his stated rules about where startups win and where they don't.

**How we get there**
1. **The closest case he discussed: winning through legal leverage.** He says startups "make the best stuff" and are strongest on level playing fields. They're weakest where incumbents win by other means: "In these worlds you don't win by having the best product." He also notes that record labels and PBMs "are full of lawyers," and says that's presumably a way to recognise such companies. ([[web-19ac0b6d18d2]], [Making Startups Powerful](https://paulgraham.com/powerful.html))
2. **The rule behind it.** A startup only becomes powerful by making customers' lives better: "Newly founded startups are too weak to force anything on anyone. The only way they can become powerful is to make customers' lives better." Every strategic move "has to make things better for the customer." (same essay) A patent is a way to force something on someone, namely to stop a competitor. That doesn't make anything better for the customer.
3. **How the patent case fits the rule.** If the patent is the main advantage, the company is trying to win by a means other than having the best product. PG would treat that as a warning sign, much like "playing house" (going through the motions of a startup instead of building what users want).

**Why he'd say it**
- He thinks you can't game your way to success: "Starting a startup is where gaming the system stops working." "So, you have to have something people want. And you only prosper to the extend that you do." "There are tricks in the startups … But they are an order of magnitude less important than solving the real problem." ([[yt-ii1jcLg-eIQ]] @ 11:00–13:17, [video](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ii1jcLg-eIQ&t=660s))
- He thinks a weaker product loses outright, patent or not: "If your product is only half as good as your competitor's, you don't get half as many customers. You get no customers." ([[web-76d87c7c2e80]], [Superlinear Returns](https://paulgraham.com/superlinear.html))
- The defenses he does name are growth and network effects: "in a market with network effects, a company that grows fast enough can shut out potential competitors." (same essay) Elsewhere he says the two numbers that matter are growth rate and how long it lasts, and the key is "not exploitation but empathy." ([[web-278ac10fa14b]], [How to Earn a Billion Dollars](https://paulgraham.com/earn.html))

**Beyond the vault (not in the vault):** In his 2006 essay "Are Software Patents Evil?", PG argued that patents matter little to startups. In his view, a startup's real protection is moving faster and building a better product than the big companies, and patents are mostly useful defensively. That essay isn't in this vault, so none of the quotes above come from it. It points the same way as the inference.

**What would change his answer:** If the patent protects a real technical breakthrough that users want badly, he'd see the breakthrough as the advantage and the patent as incidental. That could apply to something like a drug or a hard-tech invention, where copying is cheap and development is expensive. The difference that could break the inference is that his essays are about software and consumer startups. Patents may matter more in biotech, and the vault doesn't cover his views there.

**Vault gap:** The vault has no leaf on patents or defensibility. Fetching and compiling "Are Software Patents Evil?" (paulgraham.com/softwarepatents.html) would move this from an inference to something he said. I can do that if you want.

**Verdict:** Paul Graham would tell them they're making a mistake. Starting a startup is about the least efficient way to get famous or look cool. If it fails, you get a weak badge. If it works, it takes over your life, and you put up with years of grinding before anyone notices you.

**Based on:** mostly things he said. He talked directly about people who start startups, or apply to YC, for prestige and to "seem cool." Fame isn't word-for-word what he discussed, but it's very close (high confidence).

**Why he'd say it**

- **The status payoff is backwards.** Asked whether a startup is a good line on a résumé, he says it's one "only if it fails. If it works, it's like your life's work." ([video @ 7:44](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=5bxp78i96S8&t=464s)). He thinks people who see startups as a credential are "not thinking it through" (@ 8:18).
- **He has seen this motive before, and it went badly.** "It was quite early on in YC's history when people started applying to YC for the prestige" (@ 8:18). Unlike Harvard, "With startups, there's no easy majors," and so "these people trying to get YC trying to do YC as a credential, they had no idea what they were asking for." ([@ 8:52](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=5bxp78i96S8&t=532s))
- **Fame comes very late.** "If you want to seem cool, like starting a startup is just about the least efficient way to do it… you won't seem cool for years of years of brutal hardness before anyone will think you're cool." (@ 8:52–9:23). The vault marks these two lines as medium confidence because the transcript doesn't make clear who is speaking.
- **A goal that far away won't keep you going day to day.** He says ambition is necessary, but that "being dutiful is not enough… there's got to be something driving you" ([@ 5:32](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=5bxp78i96S8&t=332s)). He also says founders don't stay motivated by the big prize: "you're not thinking I got to deal with this because if I deal with it I'll become a billionaire" (@ 6:05). They "put your head down and work on the model train set for 10 years," and the success "takes people by surprise when it happens" (@ 6:38). Fame works the same way: it's a side effect you notice afterward, not something that keeps you working.
- **What he'd tell them to aim for instead.** Follow your curiosity, not your career: "be driven by curiosity rather than careerism" ([Superlinear Returns](https://paulgraham.com/superlinear.html)). Also: "Make good new things… the best proof that one has thought well" ([What to Do](https://paulgraham.com/do.html)). He even suggests going after work that *isn't* considered prestigious, if you can explain what everyone else is missing about it.

**What would change his answer:** He has no problem with ambition. If wanting to be famous comes along with a problem the founder really cares about and real determination ("very very hard working and clever and determined," @ 8:52), he'd say go ahead, because the fame part won't matter. What he objects to is fame being the *main* reason. In his view, someone driven by that will either quit when things get hard or get stuck in a company they never really wanted to build.

The vault has no `wiki/thinking/pg.md` page, so this answer is based only on the topic pages, mainly `founders/becoming-a-founder/is-a-startup-a-good-credential.md` and `founders/traits/what-drives-founders.md`. I haven't saved the answer anywhere. I can save it to `derived/` if you want to keep it.

**Verdict:** Paul Graham would most likely say a Web3 social network is the classic idea someone thought up on purpose: it sounds plausible but is bad. He'd want to know who is already using it and why, not which technology it runs on. That changes only if it started as something you and your friends actually use.

**Based on:** follows from what he said (confidence: medium). The vault has no PG statement on crypto, Web3 or social networks. The only crypto material is Seibel and Caldwell on Coinbase.

**How we get there**
1. **This is the kind of idea his main rule is aimed at.** People combine a hot technology with a big category on purpose: "Web3" plus "social". He warns that "if you make a conscious effort to try and think of startup ideas, you will think of ideas that are not only bad, but bad and plausible sounding." ([yt-ii1jcLg-eIQ @ 24:34](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ii1jcLg-eIQ&t=1474s), 2014). He said the same in 2024 and 2026: the best ideas come from projects done for fun, and you find them "without looking for them" ([web-278ac10fa14b](https://paulgraham.com/earn.html)).
2. **His test is who already wants it.** For young founders: "The idea doesn't have to have a wide appeal. It literally just has to appeal to you and your friends." His more general rule: "The key to starting a successful startup is to understand some group of users so well that you can make exactly what they want." ([web-278ac10fa14b](https://paulgraham.com/earn.html)). Using Web3 is a choice of technology. It doesn't tell you who the users are.
3. **Social networks are a hard place to attack an incumbent head on.** PG: "the way you make a new Google is not by attacking them head on." You wait "for things to change so much that their model is is obsolete" ([yt-5bxp78i96S8 @ 3:53–4:28](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=5bxp78i96S8&t=233s)). He also warns that when a mediocre product stays popular, "there's often a hidden reason why. Perhaps monopoly or regulation make it hard to compete." ([web-76d87c7c2e80](https://paulgraham.com/superlinear.html)). For social networks, the network effect is that hidden reason. So the question for this idea: does Web3 make the incumbents' model obsolete, or is it just a different backend?

**Why he wouldn't dismiss it outright**
- He says the best ideas sound lame at first: "Anything that genuinely seems to you like it would be a cool thing to build has a high probability of leading to a good startup idea, no matter how preposterous it sounds." ([web-278ac10fa14b](https://paulgraham.com/earn.html)). "Web3 is dead" isn't a reason he would accept for rejecting it.
- YC funded Coinbase when people called Bitcoin a bubble. In Seibel and Caldwell's telling, it won by making buying Bitcoin simple and safe, not through the ideology. Caldwell remembers that early Coinbase had "no social network". That's their account, not PG's ([yt-Jcuqq48CNj8 @ 9:50–11:31](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Jcuqq48CNj8&t=590s)).

**What would change his answer:** a group of real users, ideally the founders and their friends, who already use the thing because it does something no existing network can, with "Web3" as the reason it works rather than the pitch. Better still if it grew out of a side project instead of a pitch deck. Then it would pass his main test, however unfashionable crypto is in 2026.

**What I added from outside the vault:** PG has been publicly skeptical of crypto hype elsewhere, but the vault has no sources on that, so none of the reasoning above relies on it.

I can save this as `derived/pg-web3-social-network.md` if you want to keep it.

**Verdict:** No. Paul Graham would tell a startup not to spend its seed money on a Super Bowl ad. In his view a startup grows by making something users love and getting word of mouth going through hands-on work with a few early customers. A national ad buy is the opposite of that.

**Based on:** follows from what he said (confidence: medium). The vault has nothing from him about Super Bowl ads or paid advertising for startups. This answer applies his views on growth and on spending.

**How we get there**
1. **The nearest case: shortcuts to growth.** He calls them worthless: "Whenever you hear anybody talk about growth hacks, just mentally translate it in your mind to bullshit." The alternative he gives is "make something that users really love. Right, and then tell them about it." ([Startup School 2014 @ 10:26](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ii1jcLg-eIQ&t=626s))
2. **The rule behind it.** Growth has to come from the product spreading on its own. "To grow at a consistent rate every month, you have to make something so good that people tell their friends about it." He asks founders about their growth rate because "It shows whether they've built the right thing." ([How to Earn a Billion](https://paulgraham.com/earn.html))
3. **Applying it to this case.** A Super Bowl ad buys one spike of attention. It doesn't produce compounding monthly growth, and it can't tell you whether you built the right thing. If the product isn't loved yet, the money is gone. If it is loved, you didn't need the ad.

**Why he'd say it**
- **Do things that don't scale.** "If you pay a ridiculous amount of attention to your tiny initial set of customers, ideally you'll kick off exponential growth by word of mouth." ([Superlinear Returns](https://paulgraham.com/superlinear.html)) A Super Bowl ad is reaching as many people as possible at once, which is the opposite of that advice.
- **Seed money is for reaching a milestone.** "So you just do what you can on the money you got. As long as you can get to some kind of milestone, then you can convince investors to give you more." ([2026 interview @ 12:09](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=5bxp78i96S8&t=729s)) An ad that uses up most of the round leaves no money to reach one.
- **Other YC partners say the same about paid attention.** Dalton Caldwell says "it is shocking how little um getting press helps a startup" when YC measured the signups articles actually brought in ([2026 @ 20:28](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=7TU636F_yVQ&t=1228s)). This is Caldwell talking about press, not Graham, and press isn't paid advertising, but it fits.

**What would change his answer:** a company that already has a product people love, strong growth and plenty of money, where the ad speeds up something that's already working. That describes a late-stage company, not one spending its seed round. He would probably still ask whether the money would do more for the product. That last point is my inference, not something he says in the vault.

A note on the vault: it has no `wiki/thinking/pg.md` page yet, so I reasoned from the topic pages and the raw sources instead.
